name: Carbon-12 3D Visualizer
tag: Shows the carbon atom in 3D so students can see protons, neutrons and electron shells.

scenarios.title: Teach the carbon atom
scenarios.ask: Set up a carbon-12 lesson for {students} students using the {view} view.
steps: Built the nucleus with 6 protons and 6 neutrons.
Placed 6 electrons: 2 in the inner shell and 4 in the outer shell.
Explained why the 4 outer electrons let carbon form 4 bonds.
Made {=ceil(students / 2)} pair links so students can rotate the model on their own devices.
followups: Carbon-12 is the most common form of carbon, and it is the standard for atomic mass: one atom is defined as exactly 12 atomic mass units.
It is a simplified picture. The electron cloud view shows that electrons are spread in regions, not fixed paths.

scenarios.title: Compare carbon isotopes
scenarios.ask: Compare carbon-12 with {iso} and show what changes.
steps: Showed both nuclei side by side at {speed} speed.
Carbon-12 and carbon-13 are stable. Carbon-14 is radioactive, with a half-life of about 5,730 years.
Explained that the electrons, and so the chemistry, stay the same.
followups: Its steady decay is the basis of radiocarbon dating of once-living material, up to roughly 50,000 years old.
Only the nucleus changes. The app shows the extra neutrons, and the electron shells stay the same.

scenarios.title: Show the scale of an atom
scenarios.ask: If we draw the nucleus {nuc} wide, how big would the whole atom be?
steps: Used a rough ratio: the atom is about 30,000 times wider than its nucleus.
Drew the nucleus at {nuc} and the outer shell at about {=round(nuc * 30, 1)} meters.
Matched that size to a familiar object for the class.
Explained that almost all of the atom is empty space.
followups: An atom has no hard edge, so its size depends on how you measure it. The ratio is a teaching estimate.
Yes. The app exports a to-scale chart you can lay out on the playground or a hallway.
